title: Directions and the angkot
goal: Ask for directions, understand the answer, and get around Bandung by angkot, ojek and train.
bekal: must-know angkot lines: *kénca, Pa!* and *punten, hilir!*

dialogs.title: Paguneman — On the angkot
dialogs.intro: Rani takes a green angkot (shared minibus) for the first time, heading for Jalan Braga. She sits by the door and asks the woman next to her.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Punten, Bu. Angkot ieu ngalangkungan Braga henteu?
lines.id: Excuse me, ma'am. Does this angkot go past Braga?
lines.literal: excuse-me, Bu. angkot this pass Braga not?

lines.speaker: Ibu:
lines.text: Henteu, Néng. Ieu mah ka Cicaheum. Kedah ngalih di alun-alun.
lines.id: No, Néng. This one goes to Cicaheum. You have to change at the town square.
lines.literal: no, Néng. this [mah] to Cicaheum. must move at town-square.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Is the town square far from here?

lines.speaker: Ibu:
lines.text: Teu tebih. Kirang langkung sapuluh menit deui.
lines.id: Not far. About ten more minutes.
lines.literal: not far. less more ten minute more.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Hatur nuhun, Bu. Kumaha nyarios ka supirna upami badé turun?
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. What do I say to the driver when I want to get off?
lines.literal: thank you, Bu. how say to driver-the if will get-off?

lines.speaker: Ibu:
lines.text: Cukup nyebat kénca, Pa! Atawa punten, hilir!
lines.literal: enough say left, Pa! or excuse-me, getting-off!

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Kénca hartina kiri nya? Naha lain turun?
lines.id: Kénca means left, right? Why not "get off"?
lines.literal: left meaning-its left [nya]? why not get-off?

lines.speaker: Ibu:
lines.text: Heueuh, sabab angkot eureunna sok minggir ka kénca.
lines.id: Yes, because the angkot always pulls over to the left to stop.
lines.literal: yes, because angkot stopping-its usually pull-over to left.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Ooh. And how much is the fare, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Ibu:
lines.text: Lima rébu waé. Bayarna pas rék turun.
lines.id: Just five thousand. You pay when you get off.
lines.literal: five thousand just. paying-its when will get-off.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Are we close to the town square now, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Ibu:
lines.text: Sakedap deui. Tuh, sanggeus masjid ageung éta.
lines.id: Almost. Look, just after that big mosque.
lines.literal: moment more. there, after mosque big that.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Left here, sir! Excuse me, getting off!

notes: **Kénca** = left, **katuhu** = right. ⚠️ Learn them as a pair. A memory hook for *katuhu*: it's related to *tuhu* (loyal, true), and the right hand is the "proper" hand in local custom.
**Hilir** is what you say on a Bandung angkot for "I want to get off here." It comes from *hilir* (downstream) and has become a traffic word. *Punten, hilir!* is a line you'll say almost every day.
**Ngalangkungan** = to go past (lemes, polite); loma (casual): **ngaliwatan**. Asking *ngalangkungan X henteu?* is the clearest way to check an angkot's route.
**Ngalih** = to move, change (lemes); loma: **pindah**. To change vehicles people also say *oper* or *ganti angkot*.
**Kirang langkung** = more or less, about (lemes); loma: **kurang leuwih**. Very common for estimating distance and time.
**Eureun** = to stop. *Eureun heula!* = stop for a moment! It also means to stop doing something: *eureun ngaroko* = to quit smoking.

grammars.title: Place and direction words
body: Sundanese uses **palih** (lemes) or **beulah** (loma) for "side," and it shows up in almost every set of directions.
after: Notice the ending **-eun** again, with a different job here: attached to a place word, it means "in that position relative to something." *Hareup* = front; *hareupeun sakola* = in front of the school. Same pattern: *tukangeun* (behind), *gigireun* (beside), *handapeun* (under), *luhureun* (on top of).

⚠️ Sundanese directions usually use landmarks, not street names: *sanggeus masjid*, *hareupeun Indomaret*, *palih katuhu apotek*. If you ask using a street name and the answer names buildings, nobody misunderstood you. That's just how it's done.

blocks.title: Questions to ask
items: **Punten, badé naros. Jalan Braga palih mana?** — Excuse me, may I ask? Which way is Jalan Braga?
**Kumaha jalanna ka ____?** — How do I get to ____?
**Tebih teu ti dieu?** — Is it far from here?
**Angkot naon nu ka ____?** — Which angkot goes to ____?
**Ieu ngalangkungan ____ henteu?** — Does this go past ____?
**Turunna di mana?** — Where do I get off?
**Ongkosna sabaraha?** — How much is the fare?

blocks.text: The answers you hear are usually short and full of place words. Here are some typical ones, with translations:

head: What you'll hear
Meaning
rows: Go straight, you'll come to a crossroads.
On the left, next to the pharmacy.
You need to go back a little.
It's close, you'll be there in no time.
It's far, better take an angkot.
Get off at the crossroads, then walk.
*Duka teuing, abdi ogé sanés urang dieu.*
No idea, I'm not from around here either.

blocks.title: Lines for inside the vehicle
items: **Kénca, Pa!** — Left here, sir! (asking to stop)
**Eureun heula, Pa.** — Stop for a moment, sir.
**Punten, tiasa geser sakedik?** — Excuse me, could you move over a bit?
**Ieu artosna, Pa. Nuhun.** — Here's the money, sir. Thanks.
**Aya kembalian teu?** — Do you have change?
**Macét pisan nya poé ieu.** — Traffic's really bad today, huh.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Bandung angkots are told apart by the **color** and the **route** painted on the side, not by number. Ask *angkot naon nu ka Dago?* and you'll get a color: *nu héjo* (the green one), *nu konéng* (the yellow one). Memorizing the two or three route colors you use every day is more useful than learning street names.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: kénca — lempeng — hareupeun — gigireun — caket — balik deui

Ieu ngalangkungan Braga henteu? — Tebih teu ti dieu? — Punten, hilir! — Ongkosna sabaraha? — Ka katuhu sanggeus masjid.
